It is — and it's worth naming *why*, because it's not luck and it's not polish. Every pixel-perfect behavior you're feeling comes from one architectural fact: **position is a single real number in program state, and everything else is a derivation of it.**

- The extent is a sum of exact sizes (seeded by `measureText`, corrected by one-shot capture).
- The thumb is `position / (extent − container)` — a pure derivation.
- The drag is the *inverse* of that same expression — so it lands where it points, by construction, not by tuning.
- The creep is `speed × Δt` integrated into that same number — so 50 means 50.2 measured, and a slider change is just a new coefficient on the next frame.
- Quantization happens exactly once, at the final render write — and even there only at rest, never during motion.

There's no second copy of the truth anywhere for error to accumulate in. Native scroll can't do this because the browser owns the number and hands you a rounded view of it; most virtual scrollers can't because estimates and reality live in separate books that drift apart. Ours closes the loop: reality (measurements) feeds the state, state derives every surface, so the thumb, the drag, the glide, and the end of the book are all *the same number* wearing four outfits.

And notice what that is: it's the ivue model applied to geometry. One source of truth, cheap derivations everywhere, no duplicated state. The scroller is pixel-perfect for the same reason the framework is 1.1 kB — both are what's left when you delete every second copy of a fact.

That's also why yesterday's bugs were the shape they were: every one (the hidden tail, the short drag, the CSS rename) was a place where a *second* book of truth had crept in — an estimate, an index-space map, a dead style property. Fixing them wasn't adding cleverness; it was restoring the invariant. Good sign for the article: the thesis isn't decoration, it's load-bearing.

This is not a second scroller. It is the
[vertical 1M scroller](/examples/virtual-scroller) — the same tuned
class, with the same prefix-sum cursor, origin rebasing, creep
integrator and seek pipeline — **subclassed** through its eight axis
seams. Every place the base class touches a DOM dimension or a gesture

## The reference for the module standard

`HorizontalVirtualScroller.ts` doubles as the canonical shape of an ivue
module. A class file has exactly three residents — imports, the class,
and the **namespace, which carries everything else** in canonical
section order:

- **Identity** — `$Class` (raw, for children to extend), `Class`
  (`Reactive()`, for you to `new`), `Instance` (the unwrapping-surface
  type).
- **Values** — the component contract as plain data: `propsTypes`,
  `propsDefaults`, the merged `props` (via
  [`propsWithDefaults`](/guide/extensible-components)), `emits`. Being
  data is what lets a subclass compose its surface by **spread** —
  every prop inherited, one default overridden, with the reason on the
  line.
- **Types** — all **derived** from the values (`Props`, `Emits`,
  `Slots`, `Exposed`), never hand-duplicated. Constants a module keeps
  to itself live in the namespace un-exported: private to the file, no
  module-level residue.

The SFC is pure wiring against that contract: `defineProps` receives
the runtime `props` object, so no compiler macro ever resolves a
cross-file type, and the state destructure is the only other thing in
`<script setup>`.

## Each level is a complete class

A middle class isn't scaffolding — it's a usable reactive class of its own:

```ts
const saleProduct = new SaleProduct.Class();

saleProduct.total     // 38.40 — discounted, never taxed
saleProduct.receipt() // two lines, not four
```

## Files and cycles — solved underneath

Cross-file hierarchies are the normal case, and the namespace pattern makes
them boring:

- **Every file calls `Reactive()` on its own class — safely.** The transform
  is idempotent: when `TaxedProduct.ts` processes its chain, `$SaleProduct`
  and `$Product` are already done and get skipped. Any load order produces
  the identical result.
- **Script edits rebuild coherently.** Vite and Vue reconstruct the affected
  owner from the newly evaluated hierarchy. Development uses the same
  `Reactive()` execution path as production ([Development & HMR](/guide/hmr)).
- **Import cycles are solved fundamentally, not managed.** Hierarchies grow
  into webs — products reference carts, carts create products — and webs
  eventually close into cycles. Under the namespace pattern every
  cross-module reference lives in a getter or method body: code that runs at
  **first access**, when every module in the cycle finished loading long
  ago. The immunity is structural, in any load order — not an
  import-ordering discipline you have to maintain
  ([Circular references resolve by construction](/guide/modules#circular-references-resolve-by-construction)).

Good tension to sit with, because both pulls are real. Let me separate the invariant from the expression, since I think that dissolves most of it.

**What the namespace standard actually protects is the *import seam*, not the file layout.** The ruling we proved on the scrollers says: a consumer or subclass reaches everything through `X.*` — one identity, contract as data, types derived. Nothing in that requires the contract to be *authored* in the same file. The thing we deleted in `VirtualScroller.ts` was same-file alias duplication — a top-level const *and* a namespace alias in one file, two names with zero payoff. A separate `XProps.ts` is a different situation: the alias lines buy file-level navigation, diff isolation, and a class file that isn't dominated by its own contract.

**The navigability argument is legitimate and it scales with surface size.** The scroller has ~14 props — an inline Values section reads fine. ChooseField's surface is dozens of documented props; as a namespace section it would sit as a 300-line block welded to a large class, and "open `ChooseFieldProps.ts`" beats symbol-searching every time. There's also the git dimension: contract churn and behavior churn separate cleanly in review when they're separate files. (Tooling does soften this — go-to-definition on `ChooseField.propsTypes` lands in the right place regardless of file — but open-file-by-name and diff legibility are genuinely file-level goods.)

**The one real danger of keeping `XProps.ts` is the second seam.** If consumers can import `contactFieldProps` directly, two import styles coexist and drift — some files speak `ContactField.props`, others speak the raw exports, and the namespace stops being the whole truth. That's the failure mode to legislate against, and it has a clean fix:

> **`XProps.ts` is private to its class file.** Only `X.ts` imports it; the namespace re-exports it 1:1 (`export const propsTypes = contactFieldPropsTypes; …`); every consumer, SFC, and subclass goes through `X.*`. The props file becomes an implementation detail of the module — a chapter, not a second book.

So my recommendation is a **two-tier rule, one invariant**:

1. **Default: contract inline in the namespace** (Identity → Values → Types) — what the scrollers, marquee, and every ordinary component do. Below roughly fifteen-odd props, a separate file is ceremony.
2. **Large surfaces: contract in a sibling `XProps.ts`,** imported only by the class file, re-exported through the namespace unchanged. The re-export block isn't duplication noise — it's the seam's table of contents, and it's where the "which file" question stops mattering to everyone but the author.

If we adopt this, two follow-ups belong to the everything-sweep: align the fields' export names to the canonical vocabulary (`chooseFieldParamsTypes` → shapes that re-export as `ChooseField.propsTypes` / `propsDefaults` / `props` / `emits`, retiring the `params`/`I*` naming so one concept keeps one name), and — later, after it's lived — a gate check that flags `*Props` imports from anywhere except the sibling class file. That check is what makes tier 2 safe permanently: it converts "please don't bypass the namespace" from a convention into an impossibility.

The IBR framing, since it's genuinely doing the work here: the invariant is *one consumer-facing seam, contract as data*. Inline-vs-sibling-file is expression, not essence — and the right expression is allowed to vary with the size of what it expresses. Killing `XProps.ts` everywhere would be confusing the invariant with one of its encodings.

Say the word and I'll encode the two-tier rule in the standard during the sweep — or apply it to the fields now as the proving ground.

It's earned — and it's worth dissecting *why* it reads this way, because none of it is cosmetic:

**One name carries the whole sentence.** Every symbol in that block resolves through `VirtualScroller.*` — `props`, `emits`, `Props<T>`, `Slots<T>`, `Class`, `Instance`. The reader never asks "where does this come from?" because there's only one answer, and the qualifier makes each line self-describing: `VirtualScroller.Instance<T>` tells you what it is, whose it is, and its generic shape in three tokens. That's the one-seam rule paying its dividend at the *read* site, not just the import site.

**It's a ritual, not code.** Five beats, always in the same order: props → emit → slots → construct → destructure → expose. Nothing varies between components except the name and the destructure list. When wiring is this uniform, deviation becomes signal — a reviewer's eye snags on anything extra, which is exactly what `script_setup_is_wiring_only` legislates and this file demonstrates. Uniformity is a measuring device, as your own article title puts it.

**The destructure is an index, not plumbing.** Grouped state refs / computed refs / element refs, it doubles as documentation of the component's reactive surface — you know what the template touches without reading the template. And each binding *is* the cached cell, so the legibility costs nothing.

**The types are derived, so they can't lie.** `Props<T>` comes from the runtime `props` object; `Instance` from the class. There is no place for the wiring's types to drift from the wiring's values — which is quietly the deepest reason it feels trustworthy.

A cast with a fence around it is fine engineering; it's casts that roam that rot codebases.

Both points connect more deeply than they look — the bug is actually an argument *for* putting centering in the stock scroller. Let me take them in order.

**The bug first, because I can name it exactly.** The showcase tracks a "delivered frontier" (`deliveredThrough`), and there's an off-by-one between initialization and the first arrival:

- On load: `deliveredThrough = centerIndexAt(0) - 1` — cards *left of* the center get checks. The center card itself: no check.
- First advance (4.5s later): `current` becomes 1, and the arriving card is computed as `centerIndexAt(1)` = **center + 1**. The stamp plays there, and when it settles, `deliveredThrough = max(…, center + 1)`.

So the resting center card is *skipped*: it never gets its own arrival moment, sits checkless while its left neighbors are checked, and then gets swept into the frontier as a side effect of its right neighbor's delivery — exactly your "one item does not, then the scroll happens with 'Delivered' and that makes the previous one also have a checkmark." The `max()` catch-up is the smoking gun.

**Why this is really a centering problem.** The showcase has to *guess* which card is visually central — `getComputedStyle`, padding subtraction, `floor(width / step)` — because the scroller only speaks start-aligned positions. Every guess site is a place for off-by-ones like this one. If the scroller itself snapped the current index to the **center**, "which card is central" stops being an estimate and becomes a guarantee: *the arriving card is `current`, full stop.* The whole `fullyVisibleCount`/`centerIndexAt` machinery — the bug's habitat — gets deleted.

**Should centering be stock? Yes, and it passes every test we hold options to:**

- **Reality precedent:** CSS scroll-snap ships `scroll-snap-align: start | center | end` — center-snapping is a first-class carousel idiom, not a showcase quirk. We'd be matching the platform's own vocabulary.
- **It's contract data, not a fork:** one prop (`snapAlign: 'start' | 'center'`, default `'start'` so nothing existing changes), riding the existing machinery — `scrollToIndex` already takes an alignment offset (`topOffsetPx`); center is `(container − itemSize) / 2` fed through it, and `snapToNearest` picks the nearest item measured from the container's center instead of its edge. Axis-neutral for free, since it's all main-axis math through the seams.
- **Edges behave themselves:** the first and last items can't center, and the existing position clamps already produce the standard carousel answer — they rest against the bounds.
- **The 1M card demo benefits too** — jump-to-#500,000 landing centered reads better than flush-left.

**The fix plan I'd propose, in order:**
1. `snapAlign` prop in the scroller contract + the centering offset in `snapToNearest`/`scrollToIndex`'s pipeline (converge loop keeps working — the offset is part of the re-applied target).
2. Drip showcase adopts `snap-align="center"`; `arriving = current` replaces the center-guessing; the estimation helpers die.
3. The init skip gets the delightful fix: on load, the center card **arrives** — the stamp plays once, then settles into its check. The frontier is then continuous forever: no card is ever swept in retroactively.
4. Verify the lifecycle live: every check must be preceded by that card's own stamp, across a full loop wrap.

Three real options, and they map cleanly:

**A — Clamp (what CSS does).** `snapAlign: center` centers within the scrollable range; items near the edges rest against the bounds and simply *aren't* visually centered. This is exactly `scroll-snap-align: center` semantics — the platform's own answer — and it keeps the scroller pure: no special cases, the existing position clamps already produce it. The cost: at the loop wrap, `current = 0` sits at the left edge, so "the arriving card is the centered card" breaks for the first few indexes.

**B — Center regardless, via padding.** True edge-centering needs blank space to trade — and we already own the mechanism: main-axis padding flows through `axisPaddingProps` into the scroll extent, which is precisely how CSS solves this with `scroll-padding`. Pad the strip by `(container − card) / 2` and item 0 genuinely centers, empty band to its left. No new scroller feature at all. The cost is visual: on a wide screen that's ~500px of emptiness hanging left of the first card for a full 4.5s beat at every wrap. Dramatic "fresh cycle" framing, but a half-empty strip is a real look to sign up for.

**C — The uncenterable ones don't arrive; they're *history*.** And here's the thing — the showcase already believes this. On page load, cards left of center are pre-checked as already-delivered history; only the center card gets a stamp. The wrap bug-free version is just: **wrap behaves exactly like load.** Reset to position 0, mark `0..center−1` as history (checks, no stamps), and the first *arrival* is the first card that can actually center. Nothing waits, nothing sits half-empty, and no card ever gets swept into the frontier retroactively — the uncenterable ones were never promised an arrival moment in the first place.

**My recommendation: A in the scroller, C in the showcase.** The split falls exactly on the purity line:

- The *scroller* ships clamp semantics because that's what centering *is* on the platform, with padding as the already-existing escape hatch for consumers who want true edge-centering. No policy about "waiting" belongs in there — waiting is a story about deliveries, and the scroller doesn't know deliveries exist.
- The *showcase* owns the delivery narrative, and C makes its one existing idea (history vs. arrival) total: every card is either pre-checked history or gets its own stamped arrival, at load, mid-loop, and at wrap, with zero estimation code. The email metaphor even endorses it — you open an inbox and the older mail is already there, read-marked; new mail arrives where you're looking.

B stays in the back pocket as a pure-CSS consumer choice if you ever want the "single card center stage" opening — it composes with everything above and costs no code.

If that split sounds right, say go: `snapAlign` prop with clamp semantics in the stock scrollers, drip showcase on `center` with `arriving = current`, wrap-as-reload, the estimation helpers deleted, and the full stamp-before-check lifecycle verified live across a loop.
